scenes.name: scientific notation in base two
scenes.visual: A 32-bit floating-point layout dissecting the number six. In binary, six is 110, which is written as 1.1 times two squared. The three fields light up: sign bit 0 (positive), 8-bit exponent biased by 127 storing 129, and 23-bit mantissa storing .1 followed by zeros, giving 24 significant bits with the implicit leading one.

beats.say: Scientific notation writes a number as a few digits multiplied by a power of ten, where the power dictates where the decimal point lands.
beats.show: Decimal example displays: '1,500 = 1.5 × 10³'.

beats.say: A floating-point number does the exact same thing in base two. Six is one one zero in binary, which is one point one times two squared.
beats.show: Binary conversion displays: '6 = 110 = 1.1 × 2²'.

beats.say: In standard thirty-two-bit floating point, the sign bit is zero for positive. The exponent field holds the power plus a bias of one hundred and twenty-seven, so two squared is stored as one hundred and twenty-nine.
beats.show: The 32-bit fields highlight: 'Sign s: 0 (plus)', 'Exponent e (8 bits): 10000001 (129 = 2 + 127)'.

beats.say: The fraction field holds the bits after the binary point. Because the bit before the point is always one, the hardware never stores it, gaining twenty-four significant bits of precision from twenty-three bits of storage.
beats.show: Fraction field highlights: 'Fraction f (23 bits): 1000...0 (.1 of 1.1)'. Formula: 'value = (-1)^s × 2^(e - 127) × 1.f'. Takeaway: 'an implicit leading one gives 24 significant bits from 23 stored bits'.

scenes.name: the trade-off between range and precision
scenes.visual: Bit diagrams comparing FP32, FP16, and BF16 drawn to scale. Exponent bits (orange) buy dynamic range, while fraction bits (gold) buy precision. BF16 preserves FP32's 8 exponent bits while cutting the mantissa to 7 bits, whereas FP16 uses 5 exponent and 10 mantissa bits.

beats.say: Range and precision are bought separately, and with a fixed budget of bits, every bit given to one is stolen from the other.
beats.show: A seesaw balance illustrates the trade-off: 'More exponent bits = greater range', 'More fraction bits = finer precision'.

beats.say: More exponent bits allow a format to reach vastly larger and smaller magnitudes. More fraction bits allow it to distinguish tiny differences between nearby numbers.
beats.show: Scale comparison demonstrates coarse wide spans versus fine narrow spans.

beats.say: Standard sixteen-bit floating point keeps ten fraction bits and five exponent bits, giving fine steps over a narrow range.
beats.show: FP16 bit layout displays: '1 sign | 5 exponent | 10 mantissa (fine steps, narrow range)'.

beats.say: B float sixteen does the exact opposite. It preserves all eight exponent bits from thirty-two-bit float, keeping its immense range while trimming the fraction to seven bits. It is simply the top half of a thirty-two-bit number.
beats.show: BF16 bit layout displays: '1 sign | 8 exponent | 7 mantissa (FP32 range, coarse steps)'. Takeaway: 'BF16 trades precision for range by preserving all 8 exponent bits'.

scenes.name: pi in b float sixteen
scenes.visual: Field-by-field bit dissection of pi in BF16: sign 0 (+1), exponent 10000000 (128 - 127 = 1 -> 2^1 = 2), fraction 1001001 (73/128 = 0.5703125). Total value equals 2 × 1.5703125 = 3.140625, off by 0.031%.

beats.say: Read field by field, pi in B float sixteen reveals the mechanics with complete clarity.
beats.show: The 16 bits of BF16 pi display: '0 | 10000000 | 1001001'.

beats.say: The sign bit is zero, positive. The exponent is one zero zero zero zero zero zero zero, which is one hundred and twenty-eight. Subtracting the bias leaves one, so the power is two to the first power.
beats.show: Sign and exponent resolve: 'sign 0 -> +1', 'exponent 128 - 127 = 1 -> 2¹ = 2'.

beats.say: The seven fraction bits spell out seventy-three over one hundred and twenty-eight. Adding the implicit leading one gives one point five seven zero three one two five.

Multiply by two, and the value is exactly three point one four zero six two five. Pi is three point one four one five nine, so B float sixteen is off by less than one thousandth, an error of barely zero point zero three percent.
beats.show: Final product: '2 × 1.5703125 = 3.140625'. Error note: 'Off by 0.00097 (0.031% error)'. Takeaway: 'seven fraction bits represent pi to within 0.031% accuracy'.

scenes.name: range and precision across formats
scenes.visual: Dual-axis comparison. Top: Logarithmic range showing FP32 and BF16 spanning 10^-38 to 10^38, while FP16 cuts off at 65,504. Bottom: Linear precision between 1.00 and 1.03 showing FP16 resolving every 0.00098 while BF16 steps every 0.0078 (8 times coarser).

beats.say: Look at the reach: standard sixteen-bit float maxes out at sixty-five thousand five hundred and four, while B float sixteen reaches ten to the thirty-eighth power.
beats.show: Top log axis highlights dynamic range: 'FP16 max: 65,504' vs 'BF16 max: 3.4 × 10³⁸'.

beats.say: B float sixteen reaches five times ten to the thirty-third power higher, completely banishing the numerical overflow that plagued early neural network training.
beats.show: Range gap callout: 'BF16 reaches 5 × 10³³ times higher than FP16'.

beats.say: The price is precision: just above one, sixteen-bit float places numbers every zero point zero zero zero nine eight, while B float sixteen steps eight times coarser.
beats.show: Bottom linear axis zooms into 1.00 to 1.03: 'FP16 step: 0.00098' vs 'BF16 step: 0.0078 (8× coarser)'.

beats.say: That is the whole bargain: deep learning forgives coarse rounding on individual weights, but requires enormous dynamic range across layers.
beats.show: Summary card balances the trade: 'Coarse 0.4% rounding tolerated; 80 decades of range required'. Takeaway: 'BF16 trades 8× coarser precision for 33 orders of magnitude in dynamic range'.

scenes.name: multiplier area versus bit delivery
scenes.visual: A comparison between significand multiplier area and real tensor core throughput. Multipliers scale with width squared: 24x24 (576) for FP32 down to 8x8 (64) for BF16, a ninth of the size. Yet on an H100, BF16 and FP16 run at the same 989.4 TFLOP/s, proving throughput is gated by operand delivery paths.

beats.say: When multiplying two floating-point numbers, the exponents add, and the significands multiply.
beats.show: Floating point multiplication diagram shows exponent adder beside significand multiplier.

beats.say: Because an eight-by-eight multiplier takes sixty-four gates versus five hundred and seventy-six for twenty-four bits, a B float sixteen multiplier is a ninth the size of a thirty-two-bit unit.
beats.show: Multiplier area boxes to scale: 'FP32: 24×24 = 576' vs 'BF16: 8×8 = 64 (1/9th the silicon)'.

beats.say: Yet on an H one hundred, B float sixteen runs at the exact same rate as sixteen-bit float, nine hundred and eighty-nine trillion operations a second, even though its multiplier is half the size.
beats.show: H100 throughput bars display: 'FP16: 989.4 TFLOP/s' and 'BF16: 989.4 TFLOP/s' tied despite 121 vs 64 gate area.

beats.say: Silicon area determines how many multipliers can fit on a die. But operand delivery wires determine how fast they can be fed numbers each tick.
beats.show: Data bus wire comparison illuminates delivery bottleneck: 'Both receive 16-bit operands over fixed buses'. Takeaway: 'operand delivery bandwidth, not multiplier area, governs tensor core speed'.

scenes.name: the accumulation safeguard and the 256 wall
scenes.visual: The mixed precision accumulation safeguard: inputs multiply in low precision, but running sums accumulate in FP32. A graph shows what happens adding one repeatedly: BF16 freezes at 256, FP16 freezes at 2,048, while FP32 continues accurately past 16 million.

beats.say: To preserve accuracy across millions of multiply-adds, modern hardware employs a crucial safeguard: low-precision multiplies accumulate into a thirty-two-bit floating-point total.
beats.show: Architecture diagram shows BF16 inputs feeding multipliers, whose outputs stream into an FP32 accumulator.

beats.say: If you add one repeatedly in pure B float sixteen, the running total stops advancing completely at two hundred and fifty-six.
beats.show: A running total plot tracks additions of 1. The BF16 curve flattens completely at 256: 'BF16: stuck at 256'.

beats.say: Above two hundred and fifty-six, the gap between consecutive B float numbers widens to two. Adding one lands on a midpoint that rounds right back down to two hundred and fifty-six, vanishing into thin air.
beats.show: Number line zoom at 256 shows points at 256 and 258. '256 + 1 = 257 rounds back to 256'.

beats.say: Standard sixteen-bit float hits the same wall at two thousand and forty-eight. Accumulating in thirty-two-bit float counts past sixteen million with zero rounding loss, protecting dot products across deep layers.
beats.show: FP16 line flattens at 2,048, while FP32 ascends linearly: 'FP32 exact to 16,777,216'. Takeaway: 'FP32 accumulation prevents running sums from freezing at the 256 wall'.

scenes.name: separating reality from marketing claims
scenes.visual: A critical examination of generational marketing. Contrasts a '9x generational gain' headline with genuine silicon architectural speedups (2x to 4x on real dense workloads), breaking down the three distinct factors behind inflated claims.

beats.say: When marketing announcements boast of nine-fold or eighteen-fold leaps between chip generations, look closely at what is being measured.
beats.show: A headline banner displays: '9× generational speed-up'.

beats.say: Those headline multiples almost always blend reduced precision, structural sparsity, and clustered network fabrics together into a single theoretical number.
beats.show: Three component bars separate out: 'Narrower precision (2×)', 'Sparsity assumptions (2×)', 'System scaling (2.25×)'.

beats.say: On identical precision and dense workloads, real silicon progress typically delivers a solid two to four times improvement per generation.
beats.show: An honest benchmark comparison reveals: 'Dense real-work speedup: 2× to 4× per generation'.

beats.say: Understanding the three physical attacks on the memory wall lets you separate true architectural advances from marketing arithmetic.
beats.show: Summary card highlights the three pillars: 'Hiding latency, tiling reuse, and precision scaling'. Takeaway: 'always inspect precision and sparsity when evaluating generational claims'.
